title: Recipe — Draggable Bottom Sheet with Detents
content:
GOAL: a sheet that rises from the bottom, can be dragged between a peek height and full height, and dismisses by dragging down.

BUILD:
1. Base frame = the underlying page. Set Overflow: Vertical.
2. Create three top-level frames for the sheet's overlay states: `sheet / peek`, `sheet / full`. Give every shared layer inside them IDENTICAL names (handle, title, body, cta).
3. On the trigger element: Open overlay → `sheet / peek`, Position: Bottom centre, Add background behind overlay ON (black 40%), Close when clicking outside ON, Animation: Move in / Top, 300ms, Ease out.
4. In `sheet / peek`, on the sheet frame: On drag Up → Swap overlay → `sheet / full`, Smart animate, 300ms, Gentle spring.
5. In `sheet / full`: On drag Down → Swap overlay → `sheet / peek`, Smart animate, 250ms.
6. In `sheet / peek`: On drag Down → Close overlay, Move out / Bottom, 200ms, Ease in.
7. Inside `sheet / full`, set the body frame Overflow: Vertical with a Fixed height, and set the CTA's Position: Fixed so it stays pinned while the body scrolls.

WHY THESE CHOICES: Swap overlay rather than Open overlay keeps the history stack clean, so Close returns to the page rather than stepping back through detents. On drag is bidirectional, which is what makes the sheet follow the finger. Smart animate between the two detents is what makes the handle and title appear to be the same objects moving.

HANDOFF NOTE: specify the detent heights as percentages of viewport, the velocity threshold that snaps to the next detent, and whether the drag is rubber-banded past full height.

title: Recipe — Toast with Auto-Dismiss
content:
GOAL: a toast that slides in, waits, and leaves on its own — or is dismissed early.

BUILD:
1. Three top-level frames: `screen`, `screen / toast-visible`. Identical layer names throughout; the toast layer exists in both but sits offscreen (or at 0% LAYER opacity — not visibility-off) in `screen`.
2. Trigger action on the button: Navigate to `screen / toast-visible`, Smart animate, 250ms, Quick spring, Preserve scroll position ON.
3. On `screen / toast-visible`, add an interaction with trigger After delay 4000ms → Navigate to `screen`, Smart animate, 200ms, Ease in.
4. On the toast's close button: Navigate to `screen`, Smart animate, 200ms, Ease in.

CRAFT:
- 4000ms is the standard toast lifetime; 2000ms is too short to read a sentence, 6000ms outstays its welcome. Anything with an action button in it should not auto-dismiss at all.
- The exit is faster than the entrance (200 vs 250) and uses ease-in.
- Use the Quick spring for entry — it is documented as the preset for toasts and notifications.
- Set LAYER opacity to 0%, never toggle visibility, or the toast will pop rather than fade.

WHY PRESERVE SCROLL POSITION: without it, showing a toast throws the user to the top of the page, which is the classic tell that a prototype was built with Navigate to.

BETTER OPTION IF AVAILABLE: build the toast in Figma Motion as an animated component with a timeline, so the enter, hold, and exit are one authored object with real stagger and exportable code.

title: Recipe — Shopify PDP Variant Picker with Live Price and Availability
content:
GOAL: one frame that behaves like a real product page — swatches change the image, price, and availability without duplicating frames.

VARIABLES:
- `selectedColor` (String, default "") — the chosen colour
- `selectedSize` (String, default "") — the chosen size
- `isInStock` (Boolean, default true)
- `unitPrice` (Number, default 4800 for £48.00 — store pence to avoid decimals)
- `qty` (Number, default 1)
- `lineTotal` (Number, default 4800)

BUILD:
1. Swatches are ONE interactive component with Unselected/Selected variants (Change to on click). Each instance also runs Set variable `selectedColor` to its literal ("blue", "sand", "black").
2. The product image is a component with a variant property bound to `selectedColor`, so the image swaps declaratively rather than through conditionals.
3. Size buttons: same pattern, setting `selectedSize`. For an out-of-stock size, additionally Set `isInStock` to false.
4. Price text content bound to `unitPrice`; total bound to `lineTotal`.
5. Quantity stepper: plus → Conditional `if qty < 10` → Set `qty` to `qty + 1`, then Set `lineTotal` to `unitPrice * qty`. Minus mirrors it with `if qty > 1`.
6. Add to cart: Conditional `if selectedColor != "" and selectedSize != "" and isInStock == true` → Set `cartCount` to `cartCount + 1`; Set `cartSubtotal` to `cartSubtotal + lineTotal`; Open overlay cart drawer. Else → Set `errorMessage` and Navigate to the same frame with the inline error state.

WHY IT MATTERS: the real UX risk on a PDP is whether variant/availability logic is comprehensible, not whether the layout is pretty. This prototype tests exactly that, and the conditional in step 6 IS the acceptance criteria for the Liquid build.

HANDOFF: state whether variant switching is client-side (no reload) or a URL change, because your prototype implies the former.

title: Recipe — Cart Drawer That Stays Consistent Everywhere
content:
GOAL: a cart badge, drawer, and subtotal that agree with each other across every screen in the prototype.

VARIABLES: `cartCount` (Number, 0), `cartSubtotal` (Number, 0), `lastAddedTitle` (String, "").

BUILD:
1. Header is a component. The badge's text content is bound to `cartCount`. The badge's visibility is bound to a Boolean, or use a conditional-free trick: a component variant property bound to `cartCount > 0` is not possible, so keep a `hasItems` Boolean and set it alongside the count.
2. Cart drawer is an overlay frame. Position: Right (Manual if you need an exact inset), Add background behind overlay ON, Close when clicking outside ON, Animation: Move in / Left, 300ms, Ease out.
3. Every 'Add to cart' anywhere in the file runs the same action stack: Set `cartCount + 1`; Set `cartSubtotal + price`; Set `lastAddedTitle`; Open overlay cart.
4. Line item quantity controls inside the drawer adjust `cartCount` and `cartSubtotal` with clamps.
5. Empty state: because `cartCount` defaults to 0, the drawer's empty variant is the initial state — design it properly, it is the first thing many users see.
6. Remove item: Set `cartCount - 1`, Set `cartSubtotal - price`, and a Conditional `if cartCount == 0` → Change to the empty drawer variant.

WHY OVERLAY, NOT NAVIGATE: the underlying page must keep its scroll position and its state. A cart that throws you to the top of the collection page is the exact behaviour drawers exist to avoid.

LIMIT TO KNOW: you cannot model an arbitrary list of line items. Hard-code two or three with their own variables. If the study depends on cart contents, prototype it in code.

title: Recipe — Filter Panel with Applied State and Preserved Scroll
content:
GOAL: filtering a long collection page without throwing the user to the top.

VARIABLES: one Boolean per filter (`filterInStock`, `filterSale`), `activeFilterCount` (Number, 0).

BUILD:
1. Filter chips are an interactive component (Off/On variants, Change to on click). Each click also runs Set variable on its Boolean (`not filterInStock`) and adjusts `activeFilterCount`.
2. Mobile: 'Filter' opens an overlay panel, Position Bottom centre, with Apply and Clear. Desktop: a sidebar with Position: Sticky so it stays visible as the grid scrolls.
3. Apply: Navigate to the filtered variant of the collection frame with PRESERVE SCROLL POSITION ON, Smart animate 250ms.
4. Clear all: Set every filter Boolean to false; Set `activeFilterCount` to 0; Navigate to the unfiltered frame.
5. The filter count badge binds to `activeFilterCount`. The applied-filter chip row above the grid is a component whose variant binds to the count.
6. Include the ZERO-RESULTS frame. It is the state that matters most and the one that is never prototyped.

CRITICAL HONESTY NOTE: Preserve scroll position makes this feel instant. In a real Shopify theme, filtering may be a URL change and a page load unless the theme does client-side filtering. Note the assumption explicitly, and if the build will reload, prototype the loading state too — otherwise you have promised something the build cannot deliver and the difference will be blamed on engineering.

DESKTOP AFFORDANCE: sticky filters need a scroll boundary. Give the sidebar its own Overflow: Vertical if the filter list is long, or it will exceed the viewport and become unreachable.

title: Recipe — Multi-Step Form with Real Validation States
content:
GOAL: a three-step form where errors are specific, progress is visible, and going back does not lose input.

VARIABLES: `step` (Number, 1), `email` (String, ""), `name` (String, ""), `plan` (String, ""), `errorMessage` (String, ""), `hasAcceptedTerms` (Boolean, false).

BUILD:
1. ONE frame per step, not one per state. Bind the progress indicator's variant or a bound width to `step`.
2. Text inputs: bind each field's text content to its String variable and make the frame a text input, so participants can actually type and the value survives navigation.
3. 'Continue' on step 1: Conditional `if email == ""` → Set `errorMessage` to "Enter your email" → Change to the error variant of the field. Else → Set `step` to `step + 1` → Navigate to step 2.
4. Bind the inline error text to `errorMessage` so one text layer serves every message.
5. 'Back': Set `step` to `step - 1`, Navigate to the previous step. Because the field values are variables, everything the user typed is still there — this is the whole reason to use variables here.
6. Terms checkbox: interactive component (Change to) plus Set `hasAcceptedTerms` to `not hasAcceptedTerms`. Bind the Submit button's disabled boolean component property directly to `hasAcceptedTerms` — no conditional needed.
7. Submit: Conditional on all required variables → success frame; else → the specific error.

WHAT THIS TESTS THAT A STATIC MOCK CANNOT: whether error messages are specific enough to act on, whether the back-and-forth loses work, whether the progress indicator matches the user's felt progress, and whether the terms gate is discoverable.

LIMIT: no format validation (expressions have no string methods). Prototype the STATES and specify the rules in handoff.

title: Recipe — Wallet Connect Flow with Signing States
content:
GOAL: prototype the moment that actually decides whether a crypto product is trusted — connecting, then signing.

VARIABLES: `isConnected` (Boolean, false), `address` (String, ""), `balance` (Number, 0), `txState` (String, "idle"), `network` (String, "Ethereum").

BUILD:
1. 'Connect wallet' → Open overlay `wallet-picker` (Centre, scrim on, close-outside ON — picking a wallet is abandonable).
2. Choosing a wallet → Swap overlay `wallet-connecting` (spinner) → After delay 1500ms → Swap overlay `wallet-approve` (the simulated wallet prompt).
3. Approve → Set `isConnected` to true; Set `address` to "0x7a3f…B21c"; Set `balance` to 2.4137; Close overlay.
4. The header is a component whose variant property binds to `isConnected`, so the entire app updates from that one action — CTA label, balance block, avatar.
5. Reject → Swap overlay `wallet-rejected` with a specific recovery path, not a generic error. This is the state that matters.
6. Transaction: 'Swap' → Open overlay `tx-confirm` with Close-when-clicking-outside OFF (never let a signing modal be dismissed by a stray click). Confirm → Set `txState` to "pending" → Swap overlay `tx-pending` → After delay 3000ms → Set `txState` to "confirmed" → Swap overlay `tx-success`.
7. Wire a `tx-failed` branch off the pending state and put it in the flow. Failure is not an edge case in crypto; it is a routine outcome.
8. Network switch: Set `network`, and use Set variable mode if network changes your colour tokens.

WHAT TO SCRUTINISE: is the amount, the recipient, the gas estimate, and the irreversibility all legible on the confirm screen without scrolling? Does the pending state say what is happening and roughly how long? Does the failure state say what to do next?

MOTION RULE: never animate a balance or an amount. Animate STATE (pending → confirmed), not numbers.

title: Recipe — AI Feature with Honest Latency and Failure
content:
GOAL: prototype an AI feature the way it will actually behave, not the way the demo video does.

VARIABLES: `promptText` (String, ""), `responseState` (String, "empty"), `hasEdited` (Boolean, false), `feedbackGiven` (String, "").

BUILD:
1. Empty state frame. Bind the input to `promptText` so participants type their own prompt — what they type is the most valuable data in the session.
2. Submit → Set `responseState` to "thinking" → Navigate to the thinking frame, Preserve scroll position ON.
3. THINKING STATE WITH REAL LATENCY. After delay 2000ms, not 300ms. Use your product's actual p50, and prototype the p90 in a second flow. If the thinking state has to hold attention for two seconds, it needs to say what it is doing — 'Searching your documents', 'Checking inventory' — not spin.
4. Streaming: three frames with progressively more text, chained with After delay 400ms each and Smart animate. Crude, but it tests whether users start reading before completion, which changes how you write the first sentence.
5. Response state with the full affordance set: copy, regenerate, edit, and a feedback control (Set `feedbackGiven`).
6. EDIT PATH. Wire it. Set `hasEdited` to true. If users must edit every output, that is your most important finding and it is invisible in a happy-path prototype.
7. THE WRONG-ANSWER FRAME. A plausible, confidently-worded, incorrect response. Give participants the task of verifying it. This is the single highest-value AI prototype state and it is almost never built.
8. The refusal / can't-help frame, with graceful degradation — partial help rather than a wall.
9. The error frame: model unavailable, timeout, rate limit.

WHY: AI products fail at the seams — latency, wrongness, refusal, and correction. A prototype that only shows a fast correct answer tests nothing that will determine whether the feature succeeds.

title: Recipe — Live Theme Toggle Across a Whole Prototype
content:
GOAL: one control that flips the entire prototype between light and dark, proving the token architecture works.

PREREQUISITE: your colour variables must be organised as Primitive → Semantic with MODES on the semantic collection (Light / Dark), and every layer in the file must be bound to semantic variables. If any layer holds a hex value, it will not switch — which is precisely the audit value of this exercise.

BUILD:
1. Boolean variable `isDark` (default false).
2. The toggle is an interactive component (Change to on click for the knob animation).
3. Same click, second action: Set variable mode → the semantic collection → Dark.
4. Third action: Set `isDark` to `not isDark` (needed only if other logic reads the theme).
5. For the reverse, either use a conditional on `isDark` to choose the mode, or give the toggle's two variants opposite mode actions.

WHAT IT EXPOSES IMMEDIATELY:
- Every hardcoded colour in the file, as a layer that does not change.
- Shadows that vanish on dark backgrounds (dark mode needs elevation via surface lightness, not shadow).
- Images and illustrations with baked-in white backgrounds.
- Text that passes contrast in light and fails in dark, especially secondary and disabled text.
- Brand colours that are legible on white and vibrate on near-black.
- Borders that disappear because the border token was 'grey-200' rather than semantic.

WHY THIS IS THE HIGHEST-VALUE DESIGN SYSTEM PROTOTYPE: it converts an abstract argument about token architecture into a two-second demonstration, and it finds every gap in one pass. Extend the same pattern to brand modes for multi-brand systems, locale modes for text expansion, and density modes.

title: Recipe — Skeleton to Content Transition
content:
GOAL: make loading feel like content resolving in place rather than a page swap.

BUILD:
1. Duplicate the content frame. In the duplicate, replace each content element with a skeleton block of the SAME size and SAME position and — critically — the SAME layer name. `img / hero` stays `img / hero`; it just becomes a grey rectangle.
2. Entry into the skeleton frame: whatever triggered the load.
3. On the skeleton frame: After delay 1200ms → Navigate to the content frame, Smart animate, 300ms, Ease out.
4. Shimmer: either an animated GIF fill on the skeleton blocks, or (better) a Figma Motion timeline on the skeleton component with a looping gradient translate.

WHY THE MATCHING NAMES MATTER: Smart animate interpolates the fill from grey to the real image and the text block from a grey bar to type in place. The layout never shifts. That is the whole point — you are prototyping ZERO layout shift, which is a Core Web Vitals commitment as much as a visual one.

DESIGN RULES THIS TESTS:
- Skeleton blocks must match the real content's dimensions. If your skeleton is three lines and the real title is one, you have designed layout shift.
- Skeletons should approximate content, not mimic it perfectly. Too-realistic skeletons are read as broken content.
- Under ~300ms of real latency, show nothing at all — a skeleton that flashes is worse than a brief blank.
- Over ~3s, a skeleton stops reassuring. Switch to a progress indicator or a status message.

HANDOFF: state the latency thresholds (when to show nothing, skeleton, or progress) and confirm the skeleton dimensions are derived from the real content box, not eyeballed.

title: Recipe — Onboarding Carousel with Drag and Progress
content:
GOAL: a swipeable onboarding sequence that feels native and tracks progress.

BUILD:
1. One top-level frame per step: `onboarding / 1`, `/ 2`, `/ 3`. Identical layer names for the persistent chrome (progress dots, Skip, Next).
2. Forward: On drag Left → Navigate to next, Push / Left, 300ms, Ease out. Backward: On drag Right → Navigate to previous, Push / Right, 300ms, Ease out. Push is correct here because the steps are siblings in a sequence.
3. Also wire On click on Next and a tappable dot row — never make drag the only path, since discoverability of swipe is not guaranteed and on desktop it is awkward.
4. Progress dots: a component whose variant binds to a Number variable `step`, or three frames with the active dot as a matching layer so Smart animate slides the indicator. The sliding-indicator version reads better.
5. Skip on every step → Navigate to the destination, Dissolve 200ms.
6. Final step's CTA → the app, Dissolve or Move in depending on whether onboarding was a layer over the app or a route.

CRAFT:
- Push, not Slide or Move in. Push moves both frames together, which is what a filmstrip does and what a swipe implies.
- Direction consistency is absolute: forward always pushes the same way.
- On drag is bidirectional, so a partial drag can be reversed — this is what makes it feel native.
- Do not auto-advance with After delay. Removing the user's control over pace in onboarding is a reliable way to lose them.

WHAT TO TEST: whether anyone reads past step one, and whether Skip is findable. Those are the only two questions onboarding prototypes usefully answer.

title: Recipe — Building a Complete State Inventory Frame Set
content:
GOAL: stop shipping screens that only work with ideal data. This is a working method, not an animation.

FOR EVERY SCREEN UNDER REVIEW, build these frames as a named set:
1. EMPTY — zero items, first-run. Must include a path forward, not just an illustration.
2. LOADING — skeleton or progress, with matched dimensions.
3. IDEAL — the mock everyone has already seen.
4. PARTIAL — some data missing. No product image, no avatar, no description, a null price.
5. OVERFLOW — the longest realistic content. A 90-character product title, a German translation, a 42-character wallet address, a name that does not fit.
6. MINIMUM — exactly one item. Grids look wrong with one card; carousels break.
7. MAXIMUM — enough items to require pagination or virtualisation, plus the affordance for it.
8. ERROR — network failure, validation failure, permission denied. Each with a specific recovery action.
9. OFFLINE / STALE — if the product has any offline or cached mode.
10. DISABLED / RESTRICTED — not logged in, not verified, region-blocked, insufficient balance.

HOW TO ORGANISE THEM: a dedicated page named 'States', one section per screen, frames labelled `[screen] / [state]`. Do NOT put these in the prototype flow; give them their own no-starting-point section so the flow stays clean.

WHY IT IS THE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE THING IN THIS MODULE: every one of these states will exist in production whether or not you designed it. Undesigned, an engineer invents it under time pressure. The state inventory is where design quality is actually decided, and it is invisible in a portfolio, which is why it is chronically skipped.

USE IT AS A CRITIQUE TOOL: ask for the state set before critiquing the ideal frame. Half of all design feedback becomes unnecessary once the states exist.
